title: How GPS Knows Where You Are Without Tracking You

sentences.text: Have you ever wondered how navigation satellites high above Earth can watch your every step?
The surprising reality is that those satellites cannot see you at all.
The Global Positioning System does not require your mobile phone to transmit any data.
It operates completely independently of any mobile telephone network or internet connection.
Even if you turn off mobile data, the system still delivers accurate location and time information.
Many people imagine that satellites in space actively monitor, trace, or track private mobile phones.
In reality, your mobile phone functions purely as a silent and passive radio receiver.
The United States Space Force owns the satellite system and operates it through Mission Delta 31.
Although the United States government maintains the constellation, anyone with a receiver can freely access it.
The system was originally created for military use before being opened to civilians across the globe.
Civilian access was authorised by President Ronald Reagan after an airliner was tragically shot down in 1983.
Early civilian signals were intentionally degraded by a policy known as Selective Availability.
This deliberate error degraded civilian accuracy to roughly 100 metres until the policy was ended in 2000.
Today, modern consumer smartphones can determine a position to within 4.9 metres or even better.
To understand how your device knows its place, we must look up into orbit.
The space segment of GPS consists of between 24 and 32 operational satellites.
These spacecraft circle our planet in what engineers call medium Earth orbit.
Each satellite travels at an altitude of approximately 20,200 kilometres above the surface of the Earth.
The satellites are arranged across 6 separate orbital planes tilted at approximately 55 degrees to the equator.
Each orbit takes approximately 11 hours and 58 minutes, completing 2 full trips every sidereal day.
The satellites are not spaced at equal 90-degree intervals along each orbital ring.
Instead, their spacing varies between 30 degrees, 105 degrees, and 120 degrees apart.
This deliberate geometry guarantees that at least 6 satellites remain visible from almost anywhere on Earth.
Day and night, every satellite continually broadcasts radio carrier waves down toward the ground below.
The transmission contains a unique pseudorandom code made of ones and zeros that receivers recognise.
It also broadcasts a continuous data message containing its exact orbital position and the departure time.
This detailed orbital data is called an ephemeris and allows receivers to pinpoint the satellite.
How does a phone turn these simple radio messages into a physical location?
The key is that radio waves travel at the constant speed of light.
Because this speed is constant, the time a signal takes to travel reveals the distance.
Your phone measures when the signal arrives and subtracts the time the satellite sent it.
Multiplying this travel time by the speed of light provides an estimate of distance.
Engineers call this calculated distance a pseudo-range because it contains small timing discrepancies.
A single distance measurement places your phone somewhere on a giant spherical shell in space.
That imaginary sphere is centred directly on the satellite at the measured distance.
Determining an unknown position by measuring distances to known points is called trilateration or multilateration.
This technique uses distance measurements rather than angles, which distinguishes it from traditional triangulation.
When distance spheres from several satellites overlap, their mathematical intersection pinpoints your location.
In advanced signal processing, time differences of arrival define intersecting curved geometric shapes called hyperboloids.
Calculating positions with this method demands timekeeping that borders on absolute perfection.
Because radio waves travel so fast, even tiny timing mistakes create massive physical errors.
A timing error of merely 1 nanosecond causes an error of roughly 30 centimetres on Earth.
To maintain this precision, every GPS satellite carries extremely stable atomic clocks on board.
An atomic clock measures time by monitoring the resonant frequency of specific atoms.
Atoms have fixed energy levels that oscillate at universal frequencies unaffected by temperature swings.
In international science, 1 second is defined as 9,192,631,770 vibrations of a caesium-133 atom.
Ground control stations monitor satellite clocks continuously and correct any tiny drift against reference standards.
Space travel also introduces relativistic effects described by Albert Einstein.
Clocks in orbit experience weaker gravity and travel at high speeds relative to Earth.
As a result, satellite clocks run 38 microseconds faster every day than clocks on the ground.
The designers of the GPS system had to programme hardware to correct for this difference.

scenes.heading: Fixing Receiver Clocks and Pinpointing You

sentences.text: If satellites need atomic clocks, how does an affordable smartphone manage to work?
Putting an atomic clock inside every mobile phone would be far too expensive and impractical.
Your phone relies on an ordinary internal clock that is not synchronised with atomic time.
This offset adds a 4th unknown variable to the navigation calculation.
To fix your position, the receiver must solve for latitude, longitude, altitude, and clock error.
Therefore, a GPS receiver requires signals from at least 4 separate satellites at once.
By processing 4 signals simultaneously, the phone solves mathematical equations that eliminate its clock bias.
Radio signals also slow down slightly as they travel through the charged ionosphere.
Receivers use specialised mathematical models, such as the Klobuchar model, to correct for this delay.
Consumer smartphones can also use assistive services like local wireless networks to improve accuracy.
High-end receivers used in surveying can even reach an accuracy within 2 centimetres.
To answer our question, your phone determines where you are without sending any transmissions into space.
It simply listens to time-stamped radio signals from orbiting atomic clocks and calculates your exact coordinates.
Next time your phone maps your location, consider the extraordinary cosmic clockwork working quietly overhead.
